title: Review: organic–inorganic hybrid S-scheme photocatalysts—structural design principles, interfacial charge dynamics and mechanistic insights into solar-driven H 2  evolution
abstract: Abstract Organic–inorganic S-scheme heterojunctions (OI-SHJ) have been developed as an emerging photocatalytic platform for the solar-driven H 2  production. In this review, comprehensive discussion is presented on the design and mechanistic understanding of OI-SHJ photocatalysts with a focus on the engineering of the heterointerface, modulation of the band alignment and the role of the internal electric field to direct charge transfer pathways. Strategies involving S-scheme structures with polymers, covalent organic frameworks, carbonaceous materials and metal–organic frameworks are explored, with a particular attention placed on the impact of molecular tuning, defect engineering and interfacial coupling on photocatalytic H₂ production. In addition, the systematic correlation of the synthesis approaches, electronic structure control and the charge transfer pathway along with the influence of structural design on photocatalytic performance, durability and carrier migration is critically discussed. Lastly, the current issues of scalable synthesis, interfacial stability and electronic modulation of solar-to-hydrogen conversion are highlighted for future perspectives of sustainable solar-to-H 2  conversion. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The increasing living standards in an expanding world population will lead to a dramatic rise of energy needs on this planet within the next 50 years. Power demand is expected to double at least from today’s burn rate of 12.8 to 28–35 TW in 2050 [ 1 ]. Fossil fuels are used to fulfill this need in conventional power production systems that lead to large quantity of harmful flue gases. In this regard, global warming, health problems such as CO 2 , NO x  and SO emissions from fossil fuels, the finite nature of supplies of fossil fuels and the potential political risks of reliance on foreign oil will add to the requirement for renewable sources of energy in meeting world demand for energy [ 2 ]. Hydrogen (H 2 ) energy is considered an ideal future fuel due to its high energy content (~ 140 MJ/kg), renewability and zero carbon emissions. Since atomic H 2  does not exist naturally, it must be produced via thermal, electrolytic or photolytic methods. Among these, photocatalytic H 2  production using semiconductor materials under solar light is especially promising due to solar energy abundance and sustainability [ 3 ,  4 ] .  Nevertheless, 90% of the conventional H 2  production is derived from fossil fuels; thus, it will intensify the aforementioned environmental problems; thereby, there is an urgent need to develop sustainable green hydrogen technology [ 5 ,  6 ,  7 – 8 ]. The photolysis of water to generate H 2  and O 2  is considered as one of the most promising avenues for addressing the world’s growing energy needs and looming environmental issues [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ]. Photocatalytic H 2  generation through the water splitting process, in particular, offers a possible sustainable approach in meeting the future energy need without causing environmental degradation, as H 2  is a clean energy carrier, and water and solar energy is unlimited [ 12 ,  13 ,  14 – 15 ]. Photocatalysis employs potential semiconductor to transform solar energy into chemical energy via redox reactions, e.g., water splitting. Upon the light illumination of semiconductor, the conduction band (CB) and the valence band (VB) emit an electron–hole (e − /h + ) pair resulting in excitation of electrons (e − ). However, these charge carriers recombine very fast, thus greatly reducing photocatalytic efficiency [ 16 ,  17 ]. With regard to H 2  generation, photogenerated e −  and h +  accumulated at the CB and VB, respectively, attribute to produce H 2  via reduction (CB) and oxidation reaction (VB). Upon light irradiation, e −  are jumped up to the VB and h +  down to the CB resulting in mobility of charge carriers move toward the surface of the catalyst. The CB potential must be more negative than the H + /H 2  reduction potential, and the VB potential must be sufficiently positive to allow oxidation reactions to occur. Hence, efficient charge segregation is significant parameter to achieve enhanced H 2  production [ 18 ,  19 ]. Nonetheless, photocatalysts have certain drawbacks that reduce their extensive exploitation in practice such as the high band gap energy, the low absorption of the visible light and recombination of e −  and h +  resulting in wastage of energy in the form of heat leading to low photocatalytic activity [ 20 ,  21 ]. Accordingly, a number of strategies have been employed in the past decade to enhance the photocatalytic performance of semiconductor photocatalysts via an appropriate textural design, noble metal doping, defect engineering, etc. [ 22 ].

Organic semiconductors are a class of semiconductor which contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen organic compounds in their composition. Organic semiconductors exhibit very good structural tunability, which can be exploited to tune their absorption spectra and photoelectric behavior to increase the efficiency of photocatalytic production of H 2  [ 23 ,  24 – 25 ]. Various organic semiconductors are employed such as carbon nitrides [ 26 ], covalent organic framework (COF) [ 27 ], covalent triazine frameworks [ 28 ], conjugated microporous polymers [ 29 ] and metal–organic framework (MOF) [ 30 ] have been employed widely. Conversely, inorganic semiconductor are the potential systems to investigate nanoscale phenomena and how functional properties are related to the size and the dimensionality. Inorganic nanoscale semiconductors such as silicon (Si), silicon carbide (SiC), zinc oxide (ZnO), tungsten oxide (WO 3 ), zinc sulfide (ZnS), aluminum nitride (AlN) and cadmium sulfide (CdS) are used to construct the building blocks [ 31 ]. Nevertheless, large band gap (more than 3.0 eV), difficult charge transfer and lack of active sites continue to limit the photocatalytic activities of reprehensive inorganic photocatalysts [ 32 ,  33 – 34 ]. The shortcomings of inorganic photocatalysts in particular, come out as the advantages of organic catalysts including long light absorption, high specific surface area and rapid charge transfer. Additionally, the organic photocatalysts also possess merits which can be attributed to presence of functional groups for better light absorption capacity, eco-friendly, tuneable band structure [ 35 ,  36 ]. However, the single-component photocatalysts, regardless of organic or inorganic semiconductors, are critically affected by the fast charge coupling (including bulk and surface recombination) because of the short transfer path. In a bid to quell this demerit, various strategies have been undertaken by international researchers in doping of elements, morphology or facet engineering, heterojunction assembly, etc. Heterojunction photocatalysts that have the merits of enhanced efficiency in charge separation, longer light absorption, intrinsic electric field and high redox potentials stand out as among these emerging strategies which have enormous application possibilities [ 37 ].

To date, the most common representative heterojunction photocatalysts include: p–n heterojunction [ 38 ], conventional type II heterojunction [ 39 ], Schottky heterojunction [ 40 ], Z-scheme heterojunction [ 41 ] and step (S)-scheme heterojunction [ 42 ], depending on the varied band positions the two adjacent semiconductor. In particular, S-scheme heterojunctions have been potentially employed to form heterojunction among organic and inorganic semiconductor [ 43 ]. The S-scheme heterojunction attains the fast separation, yet retains the strong redox capabilities and enhances catalytic activity of photocatalytic system [ 44 ]. Photocatalytic technology has a bright future in solving the issue of energy shortage; the major problem is that it has low energy conversion efficiency. The S-scheme heterojunction is efficient in exploiting photogenerated charge carriers, which improves photocatalytic efficiency [ 45 ]. Therefore, its progression is essential to the sustainable conversion of energy and environmental conservation especially in the production of hydrogen by solar power [ 46 ]. Moreover, in S-scheme heterojunction inorganic and organic semiconductors are bonded, either covalently or non-covalently, and new functionalities are added with tunable organic molecular structures. The lattices of inorganic semiconductors form a well-ordered structure that offers a favorable environment of organic molecule growth to enable the transfer of charge at the interface effectively. In the meantime, the use of organic semiconductors allows manipulation of molecular chromophore structures and produces photocatalysts with high light harvesting efficiency. The S band design and electronic characteristics of these hybrids facilitate the photoreactivity of these hybrids, whereas the optimization of the structural components and assembly strategies further refines the knowledge on structure–activity correlation of the OI-SHJ photocatalysts as illustrated in (Fig.  1 ) [ 47 ,  48 ,  49 ,  50 – 51 ]. Figure 1 Mechanistic illustration of OI-SHJ photocatalysis for H 2  generation.

In this review, the correlation between synthesis, structure and activity of organic–inorganic hybrid photocatalysts in relation to charge transfer efficiency, the reported literature of organic–inorganic hybrid photocatalysts in hydrogen evolution was critically reviewed. Zhang et al.,[ 52 ] created an S-scheme heterojunction between covalent triazine frameworks (CTFs) and TiO 2  and were able to demonstrate an increase in interfacial charge migration and visible light absorption. Li and his co-workers [ 46 ] developed g-C 3 N 4 /TiO 2  and g-C 3 N 4 /metal sulfide hybrids, in which band modulation and defect engineering led to a great enhancement of the H 2  evolution activity. On the same note, Cheng and colleagues [ 53 ] demonstrated MOF-derived metal oxides combined with conjugated organic polymers, where close interfacial contact was used to enhance directional e −  transport and redox potential. All these studies indicate that rational interface design between the organic donor and inorganic acceptor phases is a determining factor to inhibit recombination and maximize charge utilization.

The recent work on organic–inorganic S-scheme heterojunction photocatalysts has shown dye tuning fluorescence, charge separation and redox capabilities of NIR light absorption leading to excellent efficiency for photocatalytic applications. It has been reported that coupling organic and inorganic semiconductors to form heterostructures will improve photocatalytic efficiency for H 2  evolution, CO 2  reduction and pollutant degradation. In addition to ocean water concerns, limitations such as poor interfacial charge transfer between different phases exist when using metal oxides alone [ 54 ]. Similarly, Cheng et al. [ 53 ] is attributed to the selective recombination of low-energy carriers, which enables S-scheme heterojunctions to retain highly active e −  and h + , leading to enhanced H 2 O 2  production than conventional type II system. Furthermore, Li et al. [ 46 ], showed that reasonable band alignment for oxidation and reduction photocatalysts facilitates efficient charge migration, resulting in enhanced hydrogen production performance. Nevertheless, according to authors there are still some research gaps remained. This limited understanding of the long-term photostability of organic components under continuous irradiation and the difficulty in achieving both large-scale synthesis and interfacial engineering strategies has impeded its application. Additionally, only few reports have performed mechanistic validation through sophisticated in situ characterization methods, limiting further insight into the pathways of carrier migration in organic–inorganic S-scheme systems.

The review method consists of a systematic review of the reported systems previously regarding strategies of synthesis, interface architecture and photocatalytic testing protocols. Parameters like light absorption, band alignment, charge carrier lifetime and rate of H 2  production were comparatively analyzed to determine important descriptors that determine photocatalytic efficiency. Unlike previous collections, where one individual hybrid system of organic and inorganic S-schemes is given, the review is mechanistic and comparative of organic–inorganic S-schemes. Our work is unique in laying out design principles, which correlates the molecular tunability of organic semiconductors to the redox stability of inorganic components to present a consistent guideline on the development of the next-generation hybrid photocatalysts with enhanced H 2  evolution activity and stability.

sections.heading: Designing of S-scheme heterojunction
paragraphs: The photocatalytic hydrogen generation involves four major steps including (1) upon the irradiation of light on semiconductor (hv ≥ Eg), the light-induced e − /h +  are produced wherein upon the absorption of energy the e −  are transported to CB and on the contrary the h +  generated are migrated to respective VB of the semiconductor; (2) part of e − /h +  generated are migrated to the surface of the photocatalytic semiconductor; (3) the leftover light-induced e − /h +  recombines with the h + ; and (4) the light-induced e − /h +  migrated to the surface of the semiconductor results the oxidation reduction reaction wherein light-induced e −  reduces hydrogen ions to H 2  gas as depicted in Fig.  2  [ 2 ,  55 ,  56 ]. Figure 2 Schematic representation of charge transfer pathway in S-scheme H2 production.

sections.heading: Principle of S-scheme heterojunction for H 2  production
paragraphs: As mentioned above, the light-induced e −  and h +  must be optimally utilized in surface redox reactions for effective H 2  generation. For S-scheme photocatalysis, it is the stepwise charge transfer process, which specifically traps the high-energy e −  and h + . These trapped e − , then, reduce protons to H 2 , whereas h +  work in the oxidation reaction. The interfacial charge recombination additionally contribute to the reduction of total recombination losses. Accordingly, the S-scheme strategy endows strong redox capability and intimate interfacial charge separation, for achieving high photocatalytic H 2  evolution [ 57 ]. The S-scheme charge transfer pathway proceeds through the following three sequential steps: Formation of IEF and band alignment: Prior to the contact of the two semiconductors, Fermi level (EF) and CB of reduction photocatalyst (RP) are higher than those of the OP. In  p -type or  n -type semiconductors, if the energetic ordering allows for such an alignment. e −  spontaneously flow from the RP to the OP when RP and OP are in contact because the Fermi levels are required to be the same by the energy difference. This current flow causes formation of a region of positive charge in RP and, negative charge accumulation in the OP, resulting in space charge region formation at interface and creation of IEF which points from RP to OP. However, this transfer results in bending of band, wherein RP bands bend upward and the OP bands bend downward with the Fermi level of each band type aligning at equilibrium. Selective photogenerated carrier recombination and retention: Upon light irradiation, the two semiconductors can absorb photons and photoexcitation takes place. The VB e −  are augmented to the CB, creating h +  in the VB. However, the band bending, internal electric field (IEF) and Coulombic force lead to a recombination at the heterojunction interface with e −  of OP (CB) recombining with h +  of RP (VB). Spatially separated redox reactions for H 2  production: For a rapid segregation of charges, the oxidation and reduction processes. The strong reducing power along with high energy of backscattered CB electron reduces protons (H⁺) into H 2  on the RP side.
Simultaneously, the h +  in the VB of OP, having strong oxidizing potential, drive the oxidation half-reaction. If water is the e −  donor, this involves the oxidation of water to oxygen:

The h + , in some systems, can also be scavenged for by scavengers. IEF, bending of energy bands and coulombic interactions collectively contribute to spatially segregate the charge carriers [ 58 ,  59 ].

sections.heading: Criteria for organic–inorganic scheme heterojunction
paragraphs: The inorganic semiconductors can be classified as either  n  type or  p  type, on the basis of presence of free charge carriers. The S-scheme heterojunction was originally referred to as a heterojunction made of two  n -type semiconductors, composed reduction photocatalyst (RP) CB (more negative value) with and Fermi level (Ef) and the other an oxidation photocatalyst (OP) with a higher VB potential [ 60 ]. By comparison, organic semiconductors consist of primarily conjugated polymers, including material such as MOFs [ 61 ], and covalent triazine frameworks (CTFs), carbon nitride (CN), COFs. The majority of organic semiconductors exhibit  p -type nature due to the presence of  π -conjugated hydrocarbon framework containing electron donating functional groups, facilitating hole transport and charge carrier mobility [ 62 ,  63 ]. This basic principle of composition of S-scheme heterojunctions was also generalized to a wide range of combinations of semiconductor types, allowing the production of OI-SHJs. The relative alignment of the Ef between organic and inorganic semiconductors is the primary requirement in the construction of OI-SHJs as illustrated in Fig.  3 . Figure 3 Depiction of formation of OI-SHJs.

Fermi level of the organic semiconductor (Ef O ) is more than that of the inorganic semiconductor (Ef I ), i.e., when Ef O  > Ef I , the CB of inorganic component must be situated below the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital of the organic component. During contact, the e −  flowing out of the organic semiconductor into the inorganic semiconductor is continued until equilibrium is reached. The process causes accumulation of positive charge in the organic region and negative charge in the inorganic region to create a built-in electric field and space charge region directed between the organic and inorganic semiconductor, resulting in the bending of bands at the interface. With illumination, inorganic semiconductor photoexcited e −  recombine with h +  in the organic semiconductor under the effect of the IEF. Consequently, e −  in the organic and h +  in the inorganic phase still exist to maintain the high redox potential of the system. On the other hand, Ef O  < Ef I  should ensure that the inorganic semiconductor (CB) is positioned higher than organic semiconductor (LUMO). In OI-SHJ, Fermi level should positively correlate with a CB/LUMO position in order to guarantee that the direction of the e −  pathway is reversed between the direction of the built-in electric field. The design principles are essential in terms of the systematic design, regulation and synthesis of efficient organic/inorganic S-scheme heterojunction photocatalysts [ 64 ,  65 – 66 ].

sections.heading: Tailored synthetic approaches and interfacial assembly of OI-SHJs
paragraphs: The organic–inorganic S-scheme heterojunctions are prepared by applying organic structures or polymers to inorganic counterparts by solvothermal growth, in situ deposition or hydrothermal assembly. Strong interfacial contact is attained through covalent bonding, electrostatic attraction or  π – π  interaction, which provides effective directional charge transfer. The structural stability and alignment of the bands is added by post-treatment methods such as annealing or surface modification. The hybrid structure combines broad light absorption with high charge mobility, enabling the formation of an S-scheme pathway that preserves redox potential while minimizing e − /h +  recombination.

sections.heading: Solvothermal method
paragraphs: Solvothermal synthesis is a flexible approach employed wherein organic and inorganic precursors are allowed to react together in an enclosed vessel at elevated temperature and pressure, thereby facilitating the homogeneous nucleation and growth. Compared with traditional synthesis of organic–inorganic S-scheme heterojunctions, simply establishing a good contact interface and controllable morphology benefit charge transfer and photocatalytic activity greatly. In this regard, hollow COFs-Ph@CdS S-scheme heterojunctions were prepared by a solvothermal approach as depicted in (Fig.  4 a) with argon protection at 120 °C for 35 h and subsequent washing and centrifugation. The preparation route included the polymerization of cyanuric chloride with p-phenylenediamine in a mixed solvent system (water/ethanol) and the subsequent introduction of pre-prepared hollow CdS nanospheres, tightly contacted to form a stable organic–inorganic interface. Further, TEM analysis (Fig.  4 b and c) identified that COFs-Ph spheres exhibited a type of multilayered spherical structure with size much larger than CdS nanospheres, which could act as ideal hosts to wrap CdS. Additionally, hollow CdS nanospheres showed an average circumference of about ~ 280–300 nm and shell thickness by average of 18–20 nm. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) revealed a singular interface of hollow CdS with COFs-Ph, and lattice spacing of 0.356 nm was assigned for CdS plane. The resulting values confirmed the heterojunction construction of hollow COFs-Ph@CdS and enhancement of the interfacial area [ 67 ]. In another report, the Cu-MOFs/Mn 0.05 Cd 0.95 S composite was prepared by solvothermal synthesis, copper nitrate and trimesic acid dissolved in DMF–ethanol–deionized water mixed solution for stirring period of time and then heated with Teflon-lined autoclave maintained at 85 °C under the protection from air for 20 h. The resulting Cu-MOFs were washed, centrifuged and dried at a moderate temperature. The Cu-MOFs/Mn 0.05 Cd 0.95 S still have well-distributed Mn-doped CdS particles was fabricated, and it exhibited enhanced interfacial contact and photocatalytic performance [ 68 ]. In summary, solvothermal synthesis serves as a viable approach to fabricate organic–inorganic S-scheme heterojunctions with interfacial direct intimate contact and well-regulated morphology aiming at effective charge carrier transfer. Stable heterointerfaces, hollow architectures and the uniform particle distribution in the mentioned studies indeed played an important role to improve both structural stability and photocatalytic properties of such composites.

sections.heading: In situ  growth method
paragraphs: The in situ growth is the most common employed route to prepare organic–inorganic S-scheme heterojunctions attributing to direct nucleation of one part on another, guarantee intimate interfacial contact. This method has the advantage of suppressing lattice mismatch, prevent particles agglomeration and promoting well-dispersed heterostructures. Such significant factors result in improved charge transfer efficiency, inhibited recombination and enhanced photocatalytic H 2  regeneration. Inspired by this, the ZnIn 2 S 4 /Tp-Tta COF composite was prepared in two steps: Firstly, nanoplates of 2D Tp-Tta COF were fabricated solvothermally, and subsequently, the ZnIn 2 S 4  nanosheets were directly deposited onto them. As illustrated in (Fig.  4 d), further nanosheets of ZnIn 2 S 4  were grown on the larger-sized COF nanoplates to construct a 2D/2D sandwich-like heterostructure. SEM and TEM images (Fig.  4 e and f), indicating the ZnIn 2 S 4  nanosheets were well-dispersed and oriented nearly perpendicular to the COF plane, achieving a close connection at the interface. AFM and TEM analysis (Fig.  4 g) indicated that the composite grew in a hierarchically controlled manner to about 15 nm with ZnIn 2 S 4  coating. HRTEM images (Fig.  4 h) evidenced the crystalline structure of ZnIn 2 S 4  (d 006 = 0.29 nm, indexed to the (006) plane) and emphasized the intimate contact between nanosheets and COF nanoplates. Overall, the sandwich-like structure enhanced interfacial charge transfer, facilitated multiple light scattering and provided abundant active sites, contributing to improved photocatalytic performance [ 69 ]. In addition, the in situ growth method was also employed for preparing ZIF-67@Ni–Fe LDH composites, wherein Ni–Fe LDH particles were directly grown on as-formed ZIF-67. The precursors were dispersed in methanol and stirred at room temperature for 24 h, so that uniform LDH nucleation and growth was carried out on the ZIF-67 surface. Composites obtained were collected by repeated cleaning with methanol, and thus, the as-prepared ZNF-x samples with controlled composition and interfacial contact were obtained. However, this demonstrated that in situ growth method is versatile for fabrication of high-performance heterostructure photocatalysts with good control of the compositional loading of Ni–Fe LDH into ZnO based on the aforementioned results [ 70 ]. However, the in situ growth strategy serves as a compact road map to achieve efficient research on constructing organic–inorganic S-scheme heterojunctions with rigid interfacial coupling, uniform dispersion and controlled hierarchical architectures. Directly growing one component onto another played vital role in enhancing charge separation, interfacial e −  transfer and availability of active sites for photocatalytic H 2  evolution reactions, thus significantly boosting the overall photocatalytic H 2  evolution performance of developed composites.

sections.heading: Alternative synthetic routes for the fabrication of OI-SHJs
paragraphs: Besides the in situ growth, organic‒inorganic S-scheme heterojunctions can be fabricated by different ways. Chemical precipitation facilitates the controlled nucleation of one component on another at mild conditions, to produce homogeneous interfaces. For example, Ag 3 PO 4 /TCN heterojunction was fabricated by a chemical precipitation route, wherein g-C 3 N 4  nanotubes (TCN) were prepared by thermal polymerization of melamine and urea at 550 °C under N 2  atmosphere and the TCN was then dispersed in water with stirring for several hours, and then, the Ag 3 PO 4  solution was added to the suspension before adding Na 3 PO 4  solution dropwisely to deposit the Ag 3 PO 4  on the surface of TCNs to form heterojunction. Composites containing different amount of TCN were prepared by adjusting the ratio of TCN to Ag 3 PO 4  in the precipitation step, leading to a series of samples with increasing TCN 398 loading. It was observed pure Ag 3 PO 4  had an irregular particle with 500 nm to 2 µm in size (Fig.  5 a), whereas TCN possessed a uniform 1D nanotube (Fig.  5 b). SEM and TEM images (Fig.  5 c and d) exhibited TCN nanotubes stuck to the surface of Ag 3 PO 4  particles very closely, constituting a coherent heterojunction with intimate interfacial contact enhancing charge transfer and photocatalytic performance [ 71 ]. Single-step one-pot synthesis combines multiple precursors promoting intimate contact and ease of fabrication. In this context, Du and co-workers synthesized the WO 3 /g-C 3  N 4  composites by using a one-pot synthesis method combined with mechanical mixing. The precursors g-C 3 N 4  and WO 3  were prepared by a one-pot calcination method, in which both thiourea and ammonium metatungstate (AMT) were mixed and grinded together before being synthesized at high-temperature in an oxygen deficient atmosphere. This method contributed to the synthesis of WO 3 /g-C 3 N 4  heterojunctions with adjustable ratio. Then a range of nW + CN composites were prepared by use mechanical mixing of the pre-synthesized g-C 3 N 4  and WO 3  with various weight ratios, followed by grinding to obtain homogenous mixture. This approach enabled close contact between the components and kept the individual nature of precursors, without structural similarity due to spatial constraints; thereby, a relatively simple way was achieved to adjust the interface and composition to improve the photocatalytic activity [ 72 ].

Thermal calcination was employed for improving crystallinity as well as stabilizing electronic heterojunctions by increasing interfacial charge transfer and consequent stimulus of light harvesting ratio for improved photocatalytic performance. Hence, one-pot calcination method was used to prepare NMS/SCN composites by with thiourea and ammonium tetrathiomolybdate were mixed together and the mixture was calcined in an inert (Ar) atmosphere. A range of composites with varying NMS contents (4.3, 10.2, 15.5, 19.3 and 21.9%) was prepared by varying the amount of ammonium tetrathiomolybdate and the composition and interface between NMS and SCN could be controlled. To draw comparisons, pure SCN and NMS were prepared separately with the same precursors and in the same calcination conditions. Other control samples, including NMS/CN, MS/SCN and MS/CN, were prepared by combining the individual precursors and then subjecting them to heat, whereas NMS/SCN sample was made by merely grating NMS and SCN without heat treatment. This plan allowed measuring the impacts of S doping in g-C 3 N 4 , N doping in MoS 2  and the intense chemical bond between the ingredients on the photocatalytic activities of the composites [ 73 ].

In conclusion, the morphology, surface properties and consequently the photocatalytic activity of OI-SHJs are strongly dependent on sample preparation conditions. Solvothermal synthesis typically results in hollow and porous structures, which provide larger interfacial area for light absorbing and charge migrating, while the vertical one by in situ growth benefits the intimate contact and thus directional e −  transfer of the 2D/2D heterojunction. In a similar vein, chemical precipitation works on achieving uniform surface deposition and exposure of active sites while thermal calcination and one-pot synthesis are required for crystallinity with defect engineering, interlayer spacing as well as built-in electric field. Collectively, these structural and surface modifications inhibit charge recombination, increase carrier mobility and enable enhanced photocatalytic H 2  evolution and stability; therefore, highlighting a close relationship between synthesis strategy, morphology and photocatalytic activity. Of the wide range of approaches to fabricate organic–inorganic S-scheme heterojunctions, such as solvothermal synthesis, chemical precipitation, one-pot synthesis, thermal calcination and mechanical mixing, each of the approaches has its own merits in terms of control of composition, morphology and interfacial contact. In general, the in situ growth technique is the most suitable approach since it guarantees direct nucleation of one element on the other, high interfacial contact and effective separation of charge, thus optimizing the production of H 2  through photocatalysis.

sections.heading: Advanced characterization and mechanistic validation of S-Scheme heterojunctions
paragraphs: To design high-efficiency inorganic–organic S-scheme heterojunction photocatalysts, advanced characterization methodologies are still required in order to elucidate the light absorption, charge transfer, charge carrier separation and surface redox activity. These analyses, combined with theoretical band structure calculations, support the interfacial charge transfer pathway and demonstrate that the S-scheme mechanism works within this heterojunction system.

In situ X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (ISXPS) is one of the most notable methods, which can give real-time information about the changes in the chemical state of the surface under a light-induced stimulus or other external factors and provide an understanding of dynamic interactions on the surface. Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) provides the opportunity to map both surface morphology and local surface potential simultaneously, thus providing the opportunity to spatially visualize charge distribution at the nanoscale. Moreover, density functional theory (DFT) is a predictive theory that can be used to simulate the electronic structures and evaluate charge transfer features at the interface [ 74 ]. Collectively, these approaches have given a detailed understanding of the process of the photocatalytic behavior of inorganic–organic S-scheme heterojunctions and hence have the potential to inform the rational design of the next-generation solar-driven catalytic materials.

sections.heading: ISXPS
paragraphs: ISXPS is a sophisticated surface analysis technique that can validate the S-scheme charge transfer mechanism. By using X-rays to excite the sample surface, ISXPS induces photoelectron emission, enabling the identification of chemical composition and oxidation states through kinetic energy analysis of emitted e − . In contrast to conventional XPS, ISXPS is capable of imposing external stimuli, e.g., voltage, light or ion bombardment in real time, and dynamic chemical changes at the surface of the material under working conditions can be observed. This has made it useful in relationship of surface chemistry to material performance especially in catalysis and electronics. ISXPS offers high surface sensitivity and excellent chemical resolution, and can detect trace elements without the need for complex sample preparation. Nonetheless, it has shortcomings including only limited to small-sized samples, limited to a small number of probes into the sample, and demand high-vacuum conditions, which may be inconvenient to simulate genuine operating conditions of the real world. Also, the method can result in radiation-based material damage. With ongoing advancements in instrumentation, its role in the study and optimization of surface chemical processes is expected to expand significantly across materials science and related disciplines. Li and his co-workers reported the organic–inorganic heterojunction of perovskite and graphidyne (GCTO) coupled with Co–C chemical bonds forming S-scheme heterojunction. As depicted in (Fig.  6 a-c) the binding energies of O1s, Ti 2p and Co 2p increases upon illumination in comparison with dark conditions. On the contrary, under light irradiation, the binding energy of C1s was observed to decrease indicating decreased e −  cloud density at CoTIO 3  and increased at GDY suggesting efficient e −  transfer. The recombination e −  present in the CoTiO 3  (CB) and h +  present in the GDY (VB) under influence of built-in electric field (BIEF), band bending and columbic forces suggested the S-scheme charge transfer for the organic–inorganic GTCO heterojunction [ 75 ]. In summary, ISXPS represents a versatile method to prove the interfacial charge transfer route and time-responsive surface electronic variation in S-scheme heterojunctions under operating conditions. The general light-induced binding energy shifts observed in the GCTO heterojunction provide unambiguous evidence for directional charge migration and were consistent with the proposed S-scheme mechanism driven by built-in electric field and band bending effects. sections.heading: KPFM
paragraphs: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) a technique which involves mechanically scanning surface of material with a probe in order to map its morphology and nanoscale features, such as roughness and texture. This is further augmented by KPFM, which uses an AFM tip with an applied AC voltage to measure changes in surface potential or work function. It measures electrostatic forces between the tip and the sample compensating for it by applying a DC bias voltage allowing for an accurate mapping of the local surface potential. This integrated AFM–KPFM approach offers the possibility of obtaining both topographical and electrical information concurrently, which can be used to draw a relationship between surface structure and electronic properties. In situ AFM–KPFM potential mode can perform charge transfer studies in real time during light irradiation. It demonstrates a transfer of photoexcited e −  from oxidation to reduction photocatalyst leading to a respective increase the surface potential. This supports the S-scheme heterojunction charge transfer. Additionally, KPFM images allow for direct observation of the separation of the e − /h +  pair at the interface. In this regard, Cheng and his co-workers investigated charge separation on the surface of CdS/PT S-scheme heterojunction employing KPFM. The KPFM analysis revealed clear spatial charge separation in the CdS/polymer (CP) composite as depicted in topographic images of (Fig.  6 d-f). A surface potential difference of about 100 mV (Fig.  6 g) between PT and CdS in the dark showed that there was an inherent electric field between the two materials PT and CdS, when surface to surface. When the surface is illuminated the potential at PT drops by 29 mV, whereas CdS has a lower value of 12 mV. This asymmetry in potential change confirms the transfer of photogenerated e −  from CdS to PT. CdS, as the primary component, accumulates fewer surface charges, indicating its role as the e −  donor as shown in (Fig.  6 h). Conversely, PT shows higher charge accumulation, functioning as the e −  acceptor. These observations affirm the efficient interfacial charge transfer crucial for improved photocatalytic performance [ 76 ]. In general, the integrated AFM–KPFM method directly reveals nanoscale surface morphology and interfacial charge transfer behavior in S-scheme heterojunctions over large areas. The potential differences at the surface of CdS along with light irradiation on the two systems to absorption confirmed that due to efficient spatial charge separation and directional electron migration, these variations could theoretically validate S-scheme charge transfer pathway enhanced photocatalytic activity.

sections.heading: DFT
paragraphs: DFT integrates theory with the experiments, presenting potential for investigating photocatalytic reaction mechanisms and offering guidance in catalyst design. Its applications involve e −  predicted electronic structures of photocatalysts (band gaps, band structures, energy levels), e −  evaluations of surface reactivity (adsorption energies, reaction pathways, activation barriers) and atomic-level understanding of charge transfer processes for e − /h +  migration. Furthermore, the interplay of catalysts with reactants, effects of defects, including vacancies, interstitials and dopants, and mechanistic aspects of photocatalytic reactions, specifically intermediates and transition states. In the DFT band structure simulations, the CBM and VBM were obtained and obviously represented the redox capacity semiconductors. The density of states (DOS) calculations provides deeper insights additional on orbital contributions to the CB and VB, and explained how the doping and the defects changed the electronic structures and visible light adsorption. Work function calculations based on the electrostatic potential difference by subtracting the vacuum level from the Fermi level provided a prediction of charge transfer over the heterojunction [ 74 ].

Based on this model, DFT method was further employed to explore the interfacial charge transfer of WO 3  and g-C 3 N 4  that influenced the photocatalytic activity greatly. The estimated band gap (Eg) values of WO 3  (2.77 eV) and g-C 3 N 4  (2.68 eV) depicted in (Fig.  7 e and f) indicated their applicability for visible light-driven reactions. The higher work function of WO 3  (6.23 eV) versus that of g-C 3 N 4  (4.18 eV) promoted the e −  transfer from g-C 3 N 4  to WO 3 , thus reaching a Fermi equilibrium attributed to the formation of the BIEF along the g-C 3 N 4 /WO 3  interface. Further, at interface positively charged g-C 3 N 4  as compared to negative charges accumulated on WO 3  generating a potential difference resulted in unidirectional charge separation as illustrated from (Fig.  7  a-d). This behavior was consistent with XPS response and further verified by DFT descriptors like charge density difference and Bader charge analysis, which uncovered e −  accumulation and depletion regions at heterojunction. Looking into the layered structures of both materials, it was found that also coulomb potentials were enhanced due to such geometries, which had endowed with a higher internal field than their bulk counterparts. The synergetic effects contributed to inhibit e − /h +  recombination and improve charge transfer, subsequently resulting in the enhanced photocatalytic activity [ 77 ]. In summary, DFT calculations offer basic theoretical understanding of the electronic structure, interfacial charge transfer and photocatalytic reaction pathways in S-scheme heterojunctions. In the WO 3 /g-C 3 N 4  system, the DFT analysis showed the presence of built-in electric field and directional migration of electrons that efficiently separated photoinduced electron–hole pairs which inhibited charge recombination to promote photocatalytic activity. sections.heading: Classification of organic–inorganic S-scheme hybrid photocatalyst
paragraphs: The organic–inorganic S-scheme photocatalysts are vital in the comprehension of the structural diversity and the functioning of the photocatalytic systems. These hybrid systems are a combination of the benefits of organic and inorganic elements allowing increased light absorption, charge separation and redox reactions. This section will be focusing on major classes of organic–inorganic S-scheme photocatalysts depending on its organic constituent. They are polymer-based materials, COFs, MOFs and carbon-based system, of the classes have their structural and electronic properties which affect interfacial charge dynamics and photocatalytic efficiency. A detailed discussion on their design principles, heterojunction formation and performance enhancement strategies will be presented.

sections.heading: Polymer-based S-scheme system
paragraphs: In addition to conventional inorganic photocatalysts conjugated polymers (CPs) have also emerged as promising photocatalytic candidates for hydrogen evolution owing to their remarkable geometrical flexibility, low-cost synthetic process, scalable production capacity and tailorable chemical functionalities. Their  π -conjugated electronic backbones are excellent at light harvesting and in transporting e −  to the active sites for proton reduction. Moreover, CPs behave non-toxic and show high durability to photocorrosion during lengthy operation. After the early attention to g-C 3 N 4 , a large number of CPs ranging from a series of CTFs, COFs and CPPs to polymer dots have been developed for photocatalysis. However, most of these materials suffer from complicated synthetic processes or low visible light activity. Accordingly, seeking for a simple, stable and environmentally friendly CP-based photocatalyst to display efficient visible light response is still a key issue in the studies. To achieve highly efficient CP photocatalysts, three crucial factors need to be considered: a) a wide and strong light absorption; b) well-matched energy levels for redox reactions; and c) efficient separation and transfer of photoinduced charges. A plurality of molecular building blocks have been used by researchers to design CPs as part of their efforts to synthesize CPs with specific properties [ 78 ]. In this regard, pyrene–benzothiadiazole-based polymer (PBBP)-based polymer/CdS S-scheme heterojunction was fabricated exhibiting excellent synergy between organic and inorganic substrate. Further, the zeta potential analysis demonstrated negative surface charge of −3.37 mV for pure PBBP as compared to CdS with + 5.97 mV positive potential. However, this resulted in strong columbic interactions between PBBP and CdS promoting uniform anchoring between the two. Consequently, after the composite formation XPS revealed shift in binding energy attributed to electronic interaction at the interface. The C1s and N1s were observed to shift negatively by 0.2 eV in comparison with Cd 3 d and S2p which showed positive shift by 0.1 eV as depicted in (Fig.  8 a-d). However, this resulted in the e −  migration from PBBP to CdS under dark conditions favoring S-scheme band alignment for efficient charge transfer. The charge transfer pathway followed S-scheme as confirmed by UPS along with valence band X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (VB-XPS) revealed transfer of e −  from PBBP surface to VB of CdS combining to the h +  upon irradiation. The higher positive band potential of PBBP in comparison with CdS results in the free e −  transport from low Fermi level of CdS to higher Fermi level of PBBP until equilibrium is attained. Furthermore, due to the decreased e −  density in CdS upward and downward band banding in CdS and PBBS was observed, respectively, resulting in generation of IEF. Upon light irradiation, e −  from the respective VB of CdS and PBBP are excited to CB wherein the e −  in VB of PBBP consumed h +  present in CdS as illustrated in (Fig.  8 e). Therefore, it can be inferred that the development of PBBP/CdS heterojunction efficiently facilitated improved charge carrier dynamics with photocatalytic H 2  production efficacy of 14.93 mmol h −1  g −1  after 4 recycle test [ 79 ]. Reproduced with permission from Elsevier (License no. 6123580447222).

In another similar report, organic pyrene-based conjugated microporous polymer combined with inorganic ZnxCd1-xS semiconductor to form a novel highly efficient, non-toxic PF-((g-N 3 )-alt-(g-OH))/ZnxCd1-xS (ZPF-OH) via for efficient H 2  production. UV–Vis diffuse reflectance spectra (DRS) as depicted in (Fig.  9 a and b) of pure ZnxCd1-xS and PF-OH revealed that pristine ZnxCd1-xS showed an absorption edge at 530 nm, whereas the visible light absorption of PF-OH is stronger. The absorbance of the PF-OH and ZPF-OH systems was successively increased with polymer content, confirming the successful integration of PF-OH in semiconductor. This broadened absorption range enhanced the utilization of photons, resulting in more photocarriers e − /h +  available for H 2  production. Further, it was observed that the close band gap between ZnxCd1-xS (2.36 eV) and PF-OH (2.37 eV) resulted in the formation of an interfacial heterojunction, via which efficient e −  coupling between two counterparts is achieved. The photocatalytic H 2  evolution mechanism of ZnxCd1-xS/PF-OH confirms to S-scheme heterojunction as depicted in (Fig.  9 c). During the contact of PF-OH and ZnxCd1-xS, their Fermi levels equilibrate, leading to the downward bending of ZnxCd1-xS bands and upward bending of PF-OH bands. However, this resulted in band banding causes a BIEF in ZnxCd1-xS from PF-OH to ZnxCd1-xS. Under illumination, e − /h +  are generated in ZnxCd1-xS and PF-OH, respectively, wherein the electric field forces e −  in CB of ZnxCd1-xS to recombine with h +  in the VB of PF-OH. This configuration is beneficial for the improvement of photocatalytic activity because it can capture carriers with maximum redox potential. As e −  in PF-OH reduce protons to form H 2 , h +  on ZnxCd1-xS are scavenged by sacrificial agents to prohibit photocorrosion. Consequently, this resulted in highly reducing e −  left in PF-OH (CB) with strongly oxidative h +  remaining in the VB of ZnxCd1-xS. Furthermore, interfacial reorganization upon illumination stabilizes junction to enable good charge separation and durable H 2  generation. The ZPF-OH-5 composite showed the highest HER activity of 8.72 mmol g⁻ 1  h⁻ 1  in 0.35/0.25 M Na 2 S/Na 2 SO 3  solution and 14.71 mmol g⁻ 1  h⁻ 1  in a 10% lactic acid solution, respectively. As shown in (Fig.  9 d), after cycling for 5 times, ZPF-OH-5 possesses good H₂ production activities in lactic acid; though smaller than pure ZnxCd1-xS, which is indicative of the better usability of the composite [ 80 ]. Overall, through the rational attachment of conjugated polymer-based photocatalysts to the inorganic semiconductor, it was possible to greatly improve the photocatalytic H 2  evolution. These advancements are suggestive of the potential of custom organic–inorganic assemblies which might be clean and sustainable energy technologies. sections.heading: COF-based S-scheme system
paragraphs: COFs are crystalline and porous polymer semiconductors of the novel class of 2D materials with the merits of controlled band structure, high specific surface area and wide light absorption spectrum high porosity that are projected to be promising alternative photocatalysts in H 2  production, organic synthesis, etc. COFs also possess excellent acid and base stability, as well as stability at high temperature, which continue to make potential application in photocatalysis. The structural versatility, which can be attributed to organic building blocks and linkers enables the designability as well as post-synthetic modifications. Functionalization of these nanostructures with heteroatoms (nitrogen, sulfur and halogens) allows precise design for targeted photocatalytic applications. Additionally, COFs are metal-free materials with better atom economy, lower material costs and conform to the principles of green chemistry. Moreover, their well-defined  π -conjugated systems and perfectly ordered pore structures are beneficial for encouraging efficient e −  transfer and band gap modulation, making them excellent candidates for semiconductor-based photocatalysis [ 81 ]. In this regard, TpPa-1-COF/ZnIn 2 S 4  (ZIS) heterojunction was fabricated wherein COF provided  π -stacking skeleton for efficient H 2  production. The successful incorporation of TpPa-1-COF into ZnIn 2 S 4  was confirmed by XPS analysis, wherein C 1 s peaks at binding energies of 284.9, 286.4 and 288.9 eV designated to C–C/C = C, C–N and C = O bonds in COF framework were observed for the COF/ZIS-20% sample. The O 1 s spectrum also verified the COF incorporation by the characteristic peak for C = O and aldehyde, which did not appear in pristine ZnIn 2 S 4 . On the contrary, Zn 2p and In 3 d peaks verified ZnIn 2 S 4 , and decreased N 1 s intensity observed in COF/ZIS-20%, suggested electron donation interaction from ZIS to COF via chemical bonding. These results unambiguously illustrated that TpPa-1-COF and ZnIn 2 S 4  phases coexist in the heterojunction forming intimate interfacial contact. Furthermore, DFT calculations gave deep insights into charge transfer process in COF/ZIS heterojunction. The plane-averaged electrostatic potentials (Fig.  10 a and b), the work function of TpPa-1-COF (4.82 eV) was slightly higher as compared to ZnIn 2 S 4  (4.63 eV), leading to the e −  transfer from COF to ZnIn 2 S 4 . DOS and PDOS plots (Fig.  10  c and 10 d) indicated that the VB COF was composed of C, N and O 2p orbitals and VB of ZnIn 2 S 4  was dominated by S and In states, which corroborated to a complementary VB alignment for interfacial transfer. The optimized heterostructure model (Fig.  10 e and f) reduced lattice mismatch and intimate stacking of TpPa-1-COF (001) and ZnIn 2 S 4  (102) surfaces. Finally, we have represented charge density difference maps (Fig.  10 g and h) exhibited e −  depletion (cyan) on accumulation (yellow) on ZnIn 2 S 4 , validating a spontaneous e −  flow from COF to ZnIn 2 S 4 , which generated a BIEF and promoted S-scheme charge separation. As a result, COF/ZIS-20% was the optimal formed composite which retained its stability and crystal structure after 5 cycles which H 2  evolution rate of 853 μmol g  −1  [ 82 ]. Building on these findings, it is equally important to evaluate other COF-based heterojunctions, where similar interfacial engineering strategies have been employed to enhance charge transfer and catalytic efficiency. For instance, Sun and his co-workers coupled 2D Znln 2 S 4  and organic 1,3,5-triformylphloroglucinol-4,4′,4′′-(1,3,5-triazine-2,4,6-triyl) trianiline (Tp-Tta) COF forming 2D/2D OI-SHJs. The fabricated ZnIn 2 S 4 /Tp-Tta COF heterojunction exhibited high specific surface area (137.12 m 2 g −1 ) and pore volume (0.31 cm 3  g −1 ) as validated by Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) indicated at active sites for adsorption forming sandwich-like structure. The interfacial charge transfer between ZnIn 2 S 4  and Tp-Tta COF was investigated by ISI XPS analysis. As observed in the full spectra, all elements of Zn, C, In, S, O and N before and after irradiation further under high resolution as shown in (Fig.  11 a-c) revealed well-defined negative shift of binding energy for 1.8 eV for Zn and positive for In, 0.78 eV for C suggesting e −  transfer from Tp-Tta COF toward ZnIn 2 S 4  under light illumination. This charge transfer is indicative of the IEF mediating the S-scheme heterojunction. In addition, the optical band gap of ZnIn 2 S 4  (2.5 eV) and Tp-Tta COF (1.69 eV), calculated from Tauc plots confirmed adsorption process the surface. The work function calculations made by valence band XPS as depicted in (Fig.  11 d-f) result further validated the favorable band alignment for efficient H 2  evolution rate (9.73 mmol g −1  h −1 ) and quantum yield of 13.91% [ 69 ]. Copyright RSC (License no. 1660018–1).

To elaborate these activity trends, the intrinsic S-scheme charge transfer mechanism gave deep insights into the stability of COFs-Ph@CdS. Both degradation and hydrogen evolution results confirmed the excellent stability of COFs-Ph@CdS composites. In the cyclic TC degradation, the COFs-Ph@CdS-3 still showed 65.7% efficiency after 5 successive runs of 10 h each run, with no major structural changes, thus suggesting high stability as validated by XRD analysis. For H 2  evolution, the blank sample of COFs-Ph showed weak activity toward H 2  production (4.8 μmol, 12.0 μmol·h⁻ 1 ·g⁻ 1 ), whereas the solid COFs-Ph@CdS-1 showed significant amount of H 2  (139.1 μmol), close to 29 times that of COFs-Ph and approximately 8 times those of CdS without the exfoliated layers. Activity was enhanced by the hollow composites, up to 232.3 μmol, demonstrating the optimal configuration. Moreover, the Fermi level equilibration promoted charge redistribution at the CdS/COFs-Ph interface, which generated an IEF for S-scheme charge transfer. Upon illumination of light, e −  in the CB of hollow CdS (− 1.08 eV) and h +  in the VB of COFs-Ph (2.85 eV) spatially separated to enhance redox reactions. Consequently, this promoted the generation of radicals (·O 2 − ,·OH), the degradation of pollutants and H 2  evolution [ 67 ]. To conclude, the COF-based materials demonstrate a very high potential in the photocatalysis due to the ability to tune the structure, high amount of surface area and high chemical stability. Their  π -conjugated structure allows them to transfer charges and induce band gaps effortlessly, whereas heteroatom functionalization allows them to absorb light in the visible and improve density of active sites. Owing to the creation of inner electric fields in the COF-based systems, the S-scheme charge separation is performed well, which increases the redox activity. Altogether, COFs are a prospective type of sustainable and metal-free photocatalysts to be used in environmental remediation and energy conversion.

sections.heading: Carbon-based S-scheme system
paragraphs: Carbon-based S-scheme photocatalytic systems on have attracted a lot of interest as novel and sophisticated architectures in solar-to-H 2  conversion. Carbonaceous semiconductors (e.g., g-C 3 N 4 , graphene, carbon quantum dots) can be incorporated into the system of appropriate co-catalysts, permitting the establishment of an IEF to cause directional charge flow of individual components and maintain the potent redox of constituent components of the composite. In contrast to traditional type II heterojunctions, S-scheme systems reduce charge recombination and make the most of e −  generated by photons to reduce protons. Carbon frameworks are intrinsically tunable and chemically stable, and achieve high specific surface area, which additionally facilitates interfacial charge transfer, making carbon-based S-scheme heterostructures excellent candidates in sustainable photocatalytic evolution of H 2 . In this regard, XRD analysis gives significant idea of the effective integration of WSP into the g-C 3 N 4  structure. It was observed that pristine g-C 3 N 4  had two typical peaks at 13.4° and 27.3° corresponding to the on the plane of the (100) and (002) of the heptazine units and interlayers, respectively. Upon WSP loading, the peaks shifted to 13.1° and 26.9° indicating at the interspacing between layers was increased due to the influence of the intercalation of the W species and additional functional groups. Furthermore, the lack of specific crystalline peaks of WSP indicated its amorphous state or homogenous distribution throughout the g-C 3  N 4  structure, which is advantageous to close interfacial contact and optimized charge transfer. This structural evidence provides the basis of the improved photocatalytic reaction of the composite. Figure  12 a shows the structural, band energy profile and DOS of g-C 3  N 4 . The DOS analysis showed that the N 2p and C 2p orbitals form the major part of the VB, but the major part of the CB belongs to the C 2p orbitals. Further, work function calculations and complementary DFT results revealed that g-C 3 N 4  (0.186 Ha) has a high position CB than WSP (0.22 Ha) as shown in (Fig.  12 d and e). During the heterojunction formation, the e −  will eject out of g-C 3 N 4  to WSP until the equilibrium is achieved to cause the band bending resulting in S-scheme heterojunction. The in situ incorporation of phosphorus as depicted in (Fig.  12 b and c) further decreased the WSP band gap, as compared to pristine WS 2 , to bring shallow states within the CB, which effectively trap photogenerated e −  and increase their lifetime. This interplay only allowed directional e -  transfer but it also localized reduction reactions at the exposed W sites of WSP which are the catalytic centers of proton adsorption and H 2  desorption. Additionally, the optimized WSP/C 3 N 4 −4 sample showed efficacy of H 2  generation of 3.92 mmol g  −1  h  −1  along with repeated 5 h cycle stability with long-term H 2  production stability. This, however, indicated at the synergistic interactions between the interlayer spacing, band positioning and stable heterojunction interfaces contributed to the efficiency and long-term stability of the composite photocatalyst [ 83 ]. Expanding this approach,  n  type of semiconductor tungsten oxide (WO 2 ) is employed exhibiting good stability, facile synthesis and economical viable with low band potential of (0.4 eV) not effectively separated photogenerated carriers. Hence, to address this gap S-doped porous g-C 3 N 4  was coupled together with WO 2  to form S-scheme heterostructure (S-pCN/WO 2.72 ) with oxygen exhibiting strong IEF resulting in separation of e − /h +  pair for enhanced H 2  production. This rational design was further validated by the photocatalytic degradation studies, where the synergistic effect of sulfur doping and S-scheme charge transfer was evident. The photodegradation performance under visible light (Fig.  13  a) confirmed that 0.5S-pCN achieved an 85% TC degradation rate within 120 min, validating the role of sulfur doping. As shown in (Fig.  13  b), pristine WO 2.72  mainly contributed through adsorption owing to surface oxygen vacancies, whereas its integration with 0.5S-pCN formed a tight interface that reduced adsorption but significantly enhanced photocatalysis. The kinetic study (Fig.  13  c) further illustrated that the rate constant (k) of 0.5S-pCN was 1.3 times greater than pristine pCN, while the 0.5S-pCN/WO 2.72  (30:1) S-scheme heterojunction exhibited even higher degradation efficiency, confirming the synergistic charge transfer. Finally, Fig.  13 d demonstrates the excellent stability of the composite, as its photocatalytic performance remained nearly unchanged after three successive cycles, highlighting its robustness and practical potential. Further, the VB-XPS spectra used to determine the work functions of WO 2.72 , 0.5S-pCN and their composite. The results obtained were 6.52 eV in WO 2.72 , 5.49 eV in 0.5S-pCN and 6.02 eV in 0.5S-pCN/WO 2.72  (30:1) heterojunction, which showed that 0.5S-pCN with lower work function and therefore a high Fermi energy level than that of WO 2.72 . e −  transfer was allowed to occur between 0.5S-pCN (high EF) and WO 2.72  (low EF) upon contact until the equilibrium reached resulting in the formation of an e −  depletion layer at the 0.5S-pCN surface and an accumulation layer at WO 2.72  surface. (Fig.  13 e) depicts that this redistribution of charges produced an inward electric field that propelled the e −  produced by the photogeneration process out of the CB of WO 2.72  and into the VB of 0.5S-pCN. As a result, bending of charges took place, which enhanced the e − /h +  recombination at the interface and retained high-energy carriers to undertake redox reactions. This S-scheme mechanism ensured efficient charge separation, enhancing H 2  evolution activity [ 84 ]. In nutshell, by employing WSP and g-C 3 N 4  in combination and through the creation of S-scheme heterojunction charge transfer, separation efficiency and photocatalyst activity were greatly enhanced. The combination of optimized interlayer spacing, band positioning and IEF facilitated directionality in movement of e −  and prevented recombination, and led to an increase in the H 2  evolution and degradation of pollutants. These observations have shown the key role of the structural modulation and heterointerface engineering in developing efficient and stable carbon-based S-scheme photocatalysts in order to create sustainable solar-to-fuel conversion. sections.heading: MOF-based S-scheme system
paragraphs: MOF-based S-scheme photocatalysts provide OI-SHJs between the  π -conjugated organic linkers of MOFs and the inorganic semiconductor analog. This hybrid interface produces an intrinsic electromagnetic field that causes band bending, which makes it possible to selectively recombine low-energy carriers and still maintain high redox potentials. The organic–inorganic synergy increases the light harvesting, charge mobility and interfacial e- transfer. Consequently, S-scheme route effectively reduces recombination and optimizes H 2  evolution activity. These S-scheme junctions that are organic–inorganic provide more of a flexible approach to the development of high-performance photocatalytic systems. Based on this strategy, organic–inorganic Ni-MOF-74/BiVO 4  were prepared to perform well in the production of H 2 . Ni-MOF-74 was utilized in the composite as both a structural template and an electronic regulator, with its rhombic porous structure allowing the uniform in situ growth of Ni2P nanoparticles and peanut-like BiVO 4  to effectively inhibit particle aggregation during phosphating and to allow close heterointerfaces that facilitated charge transfer. DFT studies revealed optimized structure of Ni 2 P and BiVO 4  as depicted in (Fig.  14  a and14 b), respectively. Further analysis revealed band structure (Fig.  14 c and d) Ni 2 P, a product of the phosphate MOF, exhibited the property a metallic conductor with a large density of states at the Fermi level, whereas BiVO 4  had an indirect band gap around 2.304 eV. This complementary electronic configuration enabled Ni 2 P to serve as an e −  reservoir, enhancing the movement of e −  produced as a result of the photogeneration process away of BiVO 4 , thus increasing the carrier mobility as validated by DOS depicted in (Fig.  14 e and f). The charge transfer pathway followed S-scheme heterojunction whereby the CB potentials (−0.83 eV in Ni-MOF-74 and −0.50 eV in BiVO 4 ) as shown in (Fig.  14 g) polarized the selective recombination of low-energy carriers while preserving high-energy e −  to reduce protons to H 2 . Additionally, negatively charged Ni2P/P sites (zeta potential − 42.2 mV for 20-NBP) provided electrostatic attraction for H +  ions, facilitating efficient proton reduction. Experimental evidence including suppressed photoluminescence, prolonged carrier lifetime (~ 0.33 ns), enhanced photocurrent density, reduced Nyquist arc radius and lower overpotential strongly corroborated the improved separation and migration of charge carriers within the composite. Consequently, optimal 20-NBP system had an excellent photocatalytic activity, yielding 245.4 μmol of H 2  in 5 h that was equivalent to 4908 μmol −1  h  −1 . The stability experiments determined that the H 2  production was consistent between 2 cycles with a momentary decline in the 3rd cycle because of the degradation of EY which was regained after washing and drying [ 85 ]. In another report by Wang and his colleagues, ZIF-67 S-scheme heterojunction photocatalyst was effectively prepared by in situ growth of Ni–Fe LDH on ZIF-67. XPS was employed to identify that the incorporation of the ZIF-67 and Ni–Fe LDH into the ZNF-3 composite were successful. The hybrid structure was confirmed in the survey spectra that showed the presence of Co, Ni, Fe, O, C and N. Co 2p, Ni 2p and Fe 2p peaks were observed at 797.2 and 781.5 eV, 873.8 and 856.1 eV, and 725.0 and 714.1 eV, respectively, indicating Co 2p, Ni 2p and Fe 2p, respectively. Notably, the Co, Ni and Fe peaks variations of ZNF-3 showed that ZIF-67 and Ni–Fe LDH had an extremely strong interfacial e- transfer, which confirmed the role of MOF in improving charge redistribution. ZIF-67 offered porous d dodecahedral structured material, which avoided aggregation of Ni–Fe LDH and provided numerous coupling sites, for uniform dispersion. In the presence of visible light and EY sensitization, the e −  of EY + were transferred to CB of ZIF-67 (−1.17 V) and Ni–Fe LDH (−1.07 V) and h +  were recombined across the interface to form an S-scheme heterojunction to prevent recombination. ZNF-3 was therefore found to be more efficient in generating H 2  with the highest rate of all the samples that were tested with the highest activity at a pH of 9, and was found to be stable as the same XPS peaks were recorded after and at the beginning of reaction [ 70 ]. Therefore, it can be concluded MOF-based S-scheme photocatalysts overall are efficient in utilizing the synergistic effect between organic linkers and inorganic semiconductors to enhance charge separation, carrier mobility as well as redox stability to promote H 2  evolution systems that are highly active and stable that demonstrate the potential of MOF-derived heterojunctions in advancing solar-driven photocatalysis. sections.heading: Conclusion and future perspective
paragraphs: The accelerating progression toward sustainable energy solutions worldwide has driven the exploration and development of new photocatalytic systems for solar-to-hydrogen conversion. Of note, the organic–inorganic S-scheme heterojunctions (OI-SHJs) have attracted remarkable attention as photocatalysts that can realize strong redox capability as well as effective charge separation and broad-spectrum light absorption within one system in parallel. By combining high mechanical strength and electronic mobility exhibited by inorganic semiconductors along with the molecular designability and broad visible light adsorption by organic units the advantages of both can be synergistically integrated into a single photocatalytic system. This, however, allows e −  and h +  of higher energy to be selectively retained, whereas on the other hand low-energy e − /h +  selectively recombine at the interface. Further, IEF, induced by Fermi level alignment and band bending at the interface, is the key descriptor responsible for excellent photocatalytic activities of all multiple classes including conjugated polymers, COFs, carbonaceous materials and MOFs.

This review summarizes developing evidence of controlled synthesis in particular in situ growth and solvothermal assembly that provides intimate interfacial contact for optimized morphology and crystallinity necessary to form well-defined S-scheme pathways leading to enhanced H 2  evolution. Advanced effective characterizations such as in situ XPS and KPFM measurements and DFT calculations emerge as indispensable tools to i) validate S-scheme directionality; ii) visualize the IEF and surface potential modifications; and iii) elucidate defects, doping and interfacial chemistry control carrier lifetimes as well as adsorption sites.

Besides, organic–inorganic hybridization in OI-SHJs provides further physicochemical benefits, including structural robustness, enhanced optical response and flexible energy structures leading to better light absorption and charge carrier mobility. The synergistic interfacial interactions enable directional charge transfer and mobility, inhibit  π – π  stacking between organic framework suppresses carrier recombination of photogenerated e −  and h + , and enhance interfacial polarization which altogether determine the quantum yield efficiency and photocatalytic durability. The introduction of  π -conjugated backbones into organic frameworks that facilitate efficient charge delocalization and electronic coupling, together with the active inorganic centers for redox reactions of the domains, result in high catalytic turnover.

Specifically, defect-mediated charge separation, optimized interfacial polarization and tailored band alignment were identified as key determinants of the photocatalytic efficacy of OI-SHJs. The comparison also suggests that rational engineering of interfaces can improve light harvesting and charge transport properties concurrently to better the photocatalytic performance, by overcoming the shortcomings of traditional heterojunction systems. Future research into the quest for earth-abundant, non-toxic materials coupled with large-scale syntheses as well commonly cost-effective synthesis methods will certainly be beneficial. Long-term stability and recyclability of photocatalysts, in an extended irradiation regime are still a key requirement from the applications point of view. The precise elucidation of S-scheme pathways and interfacial carrier dynamics requires a more detailed understanding of charge transfer mechanisms that can be served with operando characterization techniques and computational modeling. In addition, the scaling up of OI-SHJs into scalable photoreactor systems will bring laboratory-scale performances closer to industrial H 2  production.

In summary, OI-SHJs create a strong interconnecting link between molecular engineering and solid-state physics with improved mechanistic understanding of charge transfer and redox kinetics within hybrid photocatalytic systems. In summary, the tunable compositions and efficient S-scheme charge transfer pathways together with enhanced visible light harvesting, structural stability and superior photocatalytic activity put OI-SHJs as some of the most promising next-generation materials for sustainable solar-to-H 2  conversion and clean energy technologies.

sections.heading: Future perspective
paragraphs: Future perspectives for OI-SHJs involve several key directions as depicted in (Fig.  15 ). Exploration of earth-abundant and non-toxic materials:  Future research should aim to substitute these costly and toxic semiconductor parts with low-cost, environmentally benign and earth-abundant materials. By focusing on sustainable photocatalysts, e.g., metal-free frameworks, biomass-derived materials and non-toxic semiconductors, the environmental compatibility of OI-SHJs is enhanced. These materials can also mitigate reliance on precious metals and improve the scalability of hydrogen production processes. Development of cost-effective and sustainable synthesis methods:  While OI-SHJs demonstrate excellent photocatalytic properties, complex protocols including the use of hazardous solvents or high energy consumption routes have yet to be widely established for their fabrication. Thus, future research should focus on green methods for their synthesis, scale production procedures, solvent-free synthesis approaches and low-temperature fabrication technologies. Development of sustainable, economically feasible synthesis methods would be indispensable for pushing laboratory-scale photocatalysts to commercial application. Enhancement of stability and recyclability:  Practical photocatalytic hydrogen production still presents the hurdle of long-term operational stability. Going forward, research efforts should target the improvement of interfacial bonding, photocorrosion resistance and structural stability during prolonged irradiation. Heterojunctions must be designed to be much more stable as well as chemically resistant so that their recyclability is enhanced and this aspect will greatly improve the applicability of OI-SHJs in continuous solar fuel production systems. Computational and theoretical modeling for rational material design:  DFT-based calculations along with machine learning-assisted simulations, artificial intelligence and other advanced computational methods can lead to the discovery of efficient OI-SHJs as well. Band alignment, charge transfer pathways, defect engineering and interfacial electronic interactions are some of the properties that can be obtained by theoretical modeling. This prediction-based methodology can empower rationally designing advanced photocatalysts with extraordinarily greater hydrogen evolution activity and better charge separation properties. Integration into practical and scalable photoreactor systems:  The vast majority of OI-SHJs that have been reported to date were characterized at laboratory scale, restricting their translational applications. However, future studies should be directed toward integrating these photocatalysts into larger photoreactor setups as well as devices for continuous-flow hydrogen production. Designing high-efficiency solar-driven reactor configurations with optimized light harvesting, mass transfer and catalyst recovery shall be the key for evolving commercially viable thermochemical solar-to-hydrogen conversion technologies in the coming future. Deep Understanding of Charge Transfer Mechanisms:  A comprehensive understanding of charge migration pathways and interfacial carrier dynamics is still required to fully optimize S-scheme heterojunction systems. Future research should employ advanced in situ and operando characterization techniques such as in situ XPS, KPFM, ultrafast spectroscopy and transient absorption analysis to directly monitor charge transfer behavior. Deeper mechanistic insights will help establish precise structure–activity relationships and guide the development of next-generation high-performance OI-SHJs.
